paragraphs: U-Nets process information at multiple resolutions, but the mathematical implications of this structure are not fully understood. This paper develops a framework that treats a finite U-Net as a truncated version of a model operating on an infinite-dimensional space of functions. That perspective connects architectural choices to established mathematical operations.

The authors prove that average pooling acts as a projection in the space of square-integrable functions. They also show that U-Nets using average pooling implicitly learn a representation in a Haar wavelet basis. These results give a precise interpretation to how the network handles information across resolutions, rather than treating pooling as merely an implementation detail.

The framework also interprets hierarchical variational autoencoders with U-Net architectures as two-step forward Euler discretizations of multiresolution diffusion processes starting from a point mass, which introduce sampling instabilities. The authors further find that these models learn a representation of time that supports sharing weights. Using this observation, they report state-of-the-art hierarchical VAE performance with half as many parameters as existing models.
neurips-2022-a-multi-resolution-framewor.tldr: A multiresolution interpretation of U-Nets connects average pooling to wavelets and enables hierarchical VAEs with substantially fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Stochastic approximation underlies many learning and optimization algorithms, but its mean squared error generally decreases only on the order of 1/n. Quasi-stochastic approximation offers a deterministic alternative for applications including optimization without gradients and reinforcement learning. Previous research had treated an error rate on the order of 1/n² as the best achievable rate for this alternative.

The paper shows that appropriate algorithm design can approach a much faster rate: O(n^(−4+δ)) for any positive δ. The qualification matters: the result approaches an inverse-fourth-power rate arbitrarily closely, rather than asserting that the exact exponent of four is attained. The authors introduce two techniques to obtain this improvement.

The analysis combines a new application of number-theoretic results with techniques adapted from stochastic approximation. The authors also specialize their theory to gradient-free optimization and test it on standard benchmarks. The central contribution is therefore a constructive challenge to the previously assumed rate ceiling: deterministic approximation can converge substantially faster through suitable design.
neurips-2022-approaching-quartic-converg.tldr: Carefully designed quasi-stochastic approximation can approach inverse-fourth-power convergence rates, exceeding the previously assumed inverse-square ceiling.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning draws on data held by different clients, but those clients may have substantially different data distributions. A single shared model can consequently serve some clients poorly. Training a separate personalized model for every client addresses a different objective, but the computational burden can become unaffordable when the client population is large.

This paper proposes detecting suitable collaboration partners and adaptively learning K models for the clients. The important choice is therefore not simply whether clients collaborate, but which clients should learn together. Maintaining a collection of models gives the method a way to accommodate heterogeneity without requiring a distinct model for every individual client.

The authors theoretically establish that the model learned for each client is a good approximation to that client's personalized model. Experiments on real-world datasets also support the method's effectiveness. Together, these findings motivate selecting collaboration partners as a way to balance individualized learning needs against the resources required to train many models.
neurips-2022-collaborative-learning-by-d.tldr: Detecting collaboration partners lets heterogeneous clients share K models while theoretically approximating their individual personalized models.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent to learn a new task from only a few trials. Many existing approaches still need access to the new task's reward function to determine what behavior is desirable. This paper studies adaptation when people instead communicate the objective through preferences between complete behavior trajectories.

The proposed method, ANOLE, lets an agent adapt by asking which of two trajectories a human prefers. This replaces the need for numeric rewards at every step during adaptation. The method extends information-theoretic techniques to choose sequences of questions that maximize information gained from human interactions while tolerating mistakes from a nonexpert respondent.

This makes query selection part of the adaptation process: each interaction is chosen to help clarify the task objective. Across a variety of meta reinforcement learning benchmarks, the authors report substantial improvements over baseline algorithms in both feedback efficiency and error tolerance. The findings support preference feedback as a practical signal for rapid adaptation, including when that feedback is imperfect.
neurips-2022-efficient-meta-reinforcemen.tldr: ANOLE adapts policies to new tasks using informative human preference queries while tolerating errors in the feedback.

paragraphs: EHRSQL is a benchmark for turning natural-language questions about electronic health records into SQL queries. Its questions originate from a poll of 222 hospital staff, including physicians, nurses, and teams responsible for insurance review and health records. This grounds the dataset in a range of information needs encountered within a hospital.

The researchers converted poll responses into question templates and manually linked them to the open-source MIMIC-III and eICU databases. They incorporated different time expressions and held-out questions that cannot be answered, also drawn from the poll. The resulting task therefore requires more than matching a question to a simple database lookup.

Models must handle requests ranging from basic retrieval to calculations such as survival rates, interpret time-sensitive wording, and use prediction confidence to distinguish answerable from unanswerable questions. The authors position EHRSQL as a practical resource for developing and assessing question-answering systems over structured health records. Its contribution is a benchmark organized around these deployment-relevant challenges, rather than a claim that healthcare deployment has already been solved.
neurips-2022-ehrsql-a-practical-text-to-.tldr: EHRSQL benchmarks medical text-to-SQL systems using hospital staff questions that require temporal reasoning, complex queries, and recognizing unanswerable requests.

paragraphs: Identifiability asks how uniquely observed data determine the underlying generative model. This paper proves identification results for a broad class of deep latent-variable models with universal approximation capabilities, including models associated with variational autoencoders used in practice. The analysis uses the observed data alone, without requiring weak supervision or auxiliary information about the latent variables.

The considered models connect to practical architectures using mixture priors and ReLU or leaky-ReLU activations, including VaDE and MFC-VAE. The central result is a hierarchy: different assumptions yield different degrees of identifiability. Certain conventional VAEs with isotropic Gaussian priors also fall within the framework as special cases.

The weakest result identifies the model only up to an affine transformation, so identification does not always mean recovering one uniquely fixed latent coordinate system. Even this qualified result partially resolves a previously raised open problem. Experiments on simulated and real data accompany the theory, supporting an investigation of when unsupervised recovery is possible without the side information required by earlier analyses.
neurips-2022-identifiability-of-deep-gen.tldr: The paper proves a hierarchy of identifiability guarantees for broad classes of deep generative models using observed data without auxiliary information.

paragraphs: Iron studies Transformer inference in a client-server setting where the client has private inputs and the server holds a proprietary model. The computational challenge is to carry out the model's operations through secure protocols. The paper targets matrix multiplication and three essential nonlinear components: Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm.

For matrix multiplication, the authors design a homomorphic-encryption protocol using a compact packing technique. It reduces communication by a factor of √m relative to the most efficient prior work, where m is the number of output rows. For the nonlinear operations, combining underlying protocols with specialized optimizations reduces communication and computation overhead by about half compared with state-of-the-art protocols.

The protocols are numerically precise and preserve the accuracy of plaintext model execution. Integrated into the Iron framework, they yield communication reductions of 3–14 times and runtime reductions of 3–11 times in experiments across several real-world datasets and models. These results show how optimizing both linear and nonlinear operations can substantially improve the efficiency of private Transformer inference.
neurips-2022-iron-private-inference-on-t.tldr: Iron combines secure Transformer protocols that preserve plaintext accuracy while substantially reducing communication and runtime in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Visual models trained with category names or captions can transfer across tasks because language covers many concepts. K-LITE explores enriching that supervision with structured external knowledge. The motivation is that information about a concept can provide useful learning signals beyond the words already attached to an image, offering a path toward sample-efficient learning.

During training, K-LITE augments entities mentioned in natural language with knowledge from WordNet and Wiktionary. This supplies additional information about the visual concepts the model is learning. During evaluation, it also augments the language used to refer to learned concepts or describe new ones, supporting both zero-shot and few-shot transfer.

The authors evaluate this strategy on image classification across 20 datasets and object detection across 13 datasets. They report significant transfer-learning improvements over existing methods. The contribution connects training and evaluation through the same knowledge-enrichment idea: external descriptions help shape image representations and subsequently help specify the concepts those representations should recognize.
neurips-2022-k-lite-learning-transferabl.tldr: K-LITE enriches language supervision and evaluation prompts with external knowledge to improve visual-model transfer.

paragraphs: Unified information extraction uses one generative language model to produce outputs for multiple extraction tasks in a shared format. LasUIE builds on this idea by adding learned structural information. Its motivation is that syntax, already useful in information extraction, can also guide a model that expresses many kinds of extraction results as generated text.

The method first post-trains an existing language model to induce different structural representations without supervision. A structural broadcaster combines latent trees into explicit higher-order forests that guide decoding. A further task-oriented fine-tuning mechanism adjusts the learned structures to fit the needs of the particular extraction task.

Across 12 benchmarks covering seven tasks, the authors report significant improvements over the baseline unified extraction system. Their analyses indicate that the model learns structural biases that adapt to the task and help address long-range dependencies and identifying boundaries. The approach therefore uses learned structure throughout generation and adaptation, connecting relationships within the input to the extraction decisions the model must express.
neurips-2022-lasuie-unifying-information.tldr: LasUIE learns and adapts structural representations to improve a single generative model across multiple information-extraction tasks.

paragraphs: Label ranking predicts an ordering of labels for each input, rather than selecting just one label. This paper studies a precise setting: inputs follow a standard Gaussian distribution, and the true ordering comes from sorting linear scores. Training rankings may be corrupted, but each pair of labels has probability less than one-half of appearing in the wrong order.

Under these assumptions, the authors design efficient algorithms that approximate the true rankings using normalized Kendall's Tau distance, a measure of pairwise ordering disagreement. They provide both proper learners, whose outputs remain within the linear sorting class, and non-proper learners. The labeled-sample bound is approximately d log(k)/ε, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed, and runtime is polynomial.

The paper also addresses the more demanding top-r disagreement loss. An efficient proper learner achieves error ε using approximately dkr/ε samples, again suppressing logarithmic factors. These results distinguish two ranking objectives and quantify how their learning requirements depend on input dimension, number of labels, and desired accuracy under bounded noise.
neurips-2022-linear-label-ranking-with-b.tldr: Under Gaussian inputs and bounded pairwise noise, efficient algorithms can learn linear label rankings with quantified sample requirements.

paragraphs: Machine teaching studies how a teacher can convey a concept through a small set of labeled examples. The number needed depends on the rules governing how teacher and learner interact. This paper investigates batch teaching, where examples are supplied as a collection, and its relationship to VC-dimension, a measure of concept-class complexity.

The authors introduce a teaching-complexity parameter called STDmin, whose model incorporates an intuitive notion of how important an example is for a concept. They prove an upper bound equal to the VC-dimension. Earlier batch-teaching work had established a quadratic upper bound for recursive teaching dimension, while a known linear bound applied to teaching with sequences.

The result depends on the newly proposed teaching model. In developing it, the authors argue that the customary criterion intended to prevent unfair teacher-learner collusion may be inadequate for some applications. They propose three desirable properties of teaching complexity and show that STDmin satisfies them. The contribution combines a sharper bound with a reconsideration of what a useful batch-teaching framework should require.
neurips-2022-on-batch-teaching-with-samp.tldr: A new batch-teaching model, STDmin, has teaching complexity bounded above by VC-dimension and satisfies three proposed desirable properties.

paragraphs: Methods that explain a trained model's predictions are plentiful, but systematic comparisons between them have received less attention. OpenXAI provides an open-source framework for evaluating these post hoc explanations. Its purpose is to make benchmarking easier to reproduce and more transparent by putting data, models, explanation methods, and evaluation tools into a shared pipeline.

The framework includes a flexible synthetic-data generator, real-world datasets, pretrained models, and feature-attribution methods. It implements 22 quantitative metrics covering faithfulness, stability or robustness, and fairness. Public leaderboards compare explanation methods across metrics, models, and datasets, while users can evaluate their own methods and add them to the comparisons.

The first release supports tabular datasets only, although the authors describe the selected methods and metrics as general enough for other modalities. The framework's contribution is standardized, extensible evaluation across several dimensions of explanation quality. This makes it possible to examine how methods behave under different assessment criteria rather than relying on isolated demonstrations.
neurips-2022-openxai-towards-a-transpare.tldr: OpenXAI standardizes explanation benchmarking with datasets, models, 22 evaluation metrics, and extensible public leaderboards.

paragraphs: Value factorization helps multiple agents learn together by relating a joint action-value function to utilities for individual agents. This paper identifies a representational problem under partial observability: an agent's ordering of its actions can impose simultaneous constraints across different states. Those constraints can restrict the functions the system can represent and cause substantial estimation errors during training.

PAC adds assistance derived from counterfactual predictions of optimal joint action selection. A new counterfactual loss uses this information to guide value factorization. The framework also uses variational inference to collect and encode the predictions from an estimated baseline, making the additional information part of the learning procedure.

For decentralized execution, the authors derive separate per-agent policies inspired by maximum-entropy multi-agent reinforcement learning. They evaluate PAC on multi-agent predator-prey and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art value-based and policy-based methods on every evaluated benchmark. The results support counterfactual assistance as a way to address the identified training constraints while retaining decentralized policies.
neurips-2022-pac-assisted-value-factoriz.tldr: PAC uses counterfactual joint-action predictions to assist value factorization and improve learning under partial observability.

paragraphs: Tracking objects in a single-camera video becomes difficult when they disappear behind obstacles for an extended period. Appearance-based trackers handle visible objects and short interruptions well, but the paper reports that state-of-the-art trackers bridge fewer than 10% of occlusions lasting over three seconds. Longer gaps create more possible ways to associate reappearing objects with earlier tracks.

Quo Vadis addresses this ambiguity by forecasting future movement. The authors show that even a small, diverse collection of predicted trajectories can substantially narrow the search for plausible associations. Instead of relying only on how an object looked before disappearing, tracking also uses predictions of where it could move.

Experiments suggest that three ingredients are crucial: reasoning from a bird's-eye perspective, maintaining a small but diverse set of forecasts, and accounting for uncertainty in localization. Applying this approach to state-of-the-art trackers improves their long-term tracking performance on MOTChallenge. The findings support trajectory forecasting as a useful component for reconnecting tracks across extended occlusions.
neurips-2022-quo-vadis-is-trajectory-for.tldr: A small, diverse set of trajectory forecasts improves long-term tracking by narrowing associations across extended occlusions.

paragraphs: Adversarially trained networks can handle perturbed training examples yet perform poorly on perturbed test examples, a phenomenon called robust overfitting. This paper studies that gap through uniform stability, which connects a learning algorithm's sensitivity to training data with its ability to generalize. The difficulty is that maximizing over adversarial perturbations produces a nonsmooth loss, blocking standard smoothness-based analysis.

The authors introduce an approximate smoothness condition with a tolerance parameter tied to the adversarial perturbation size. They show that the adversarial loss satisfies this condition and derive stability-based generalization bounds for stochastic gradient descent on the broader class of approximately smooth functions. This extends the analysis beyond losses satisfying ordinary smoothness assumptions.

For long training runs, the results suggest that robust test accuracy declines with increasing perturbation size, with the stated dependence ranging between ε√T and εT in asymptotic order. The authors observe this phenomenon in practice. They also show theoretically that early stopping, cyclic learning rates, and stochastic weight averaging promote stability, providing a common perspective on several training techniques.
neurips-2022-stability-analysis-and-gene.tldr: Approximate smoothness enables stability bounds for adversarial training and helps explain robust overfitting and stability-promoting training techniques.

paragraphs: Step-by-step rationales can improve language models on difficult reasoning questions, but collecting large rationale datasets is costly. STaR explores whether a model can build this capability from a few example explanations and a much larger collection of questions without rationales. The central idea is to turn the model's own successful reasoning attempts into training material.

The process repeats a simple loop. The model first generates explanations and answers using a small number of rationale examples as prompts. When an answer is wrong, it tries generating an explanation again with the correct answer supplied. The model is then fine-tuned on the rationales that ultimately produced correct answers, and the cycle starts again.

Across multiple datasets, STaR significantly outperforms fine-tuning a model to predict final answers directly. On CommonsenseQA, it performs comparably to fine-tuning a state-of-the-art language model 30 times larger. These results support iterative learning from generated reasoning, with correct answers providing the signal that selects which rationales enter subsequent training.
neurips-2022-star-bootstrapping-reasonin.tldr: STaR improves reasoning by repeatedly generating explanations, retaining those that yield correct answers, and fine-tuning on them.

paragraphs: Most model development begins with a chosen task and searches for a network that generalizes well on it. This paper reverses the direction: it fixes the learning model and searches for tasks on which that model generalizes. The resulting tasks provide a way to investigate what the learning framework naturally tends to capture in a dataset.

The proposed task-discovery framework optimizes a generalization-related quantity called agreement score. The authors show that the same collection of images can support many tasks that neural networks learn successfully. These tasks reflect both the learning framework's inductive biases and statistical patterns in the data, making them useful objects of analysis.

One application uses discovered tasks to construct adversarial training-test splits. By choosing which examples belong in each split, the method can cause test-time failure without altering image pixels or labels. This demonstrates how task discovery can expose vulnerabilities in generalization that depend on dataset partitioning. The paper also discusses whether the discovered tasks are interpretable to people.
neurips-2022-task-discovery-finding-the-.tldr: Task discovery searches for tasks a fixed model generalizes on, revealing biases and enabling adversarial training-test splits.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor search identifies items closest to a query, and its practical speed depends on how well the algorithm fits its hardware. TPU-KNN presents a search algorithm designed to reach the peak computational performance of Google's Tensor Processing Units. The design is guided by a performance model that accounts for both memory bottlenecks and instruction bottlenecks.

This hardware-aware perspective matters because arithmetic throughput alone does not describe all the constraints on accelerator performance. The algorithm also avoids requiring a sophisticated maintained index or tuning. The authors identify this as particularly useful for applications where the searchable data change frequently, since maintaining a complex index is not part of the method's requirements.

The paper reports better performance than state-of-the-art GPU algorithms at similar recall levels. It also provides an analytical guarantee on recall in expectation, qualifying the mathematical claim as an expected retrieval-quality guarantee. The work is available through open-source Jax and TensorFlow packages for TPU, connecting its algorithmic and hardware contributions to an implementation.
neurips-2022-tpu-knn-k-nearest-neighbor-.tldr: TPU-KNN aligns nearest-neighbor search with TPU hardware bottlenecks to achieve peak performance with an expected-recall guarantee.

paragraphs: An equivariant representation changes in a corresponding way when its stimulus is transformed. This paper asks how recurrent neural circuitry could implement such a representation, using one-dimensional translation as its example. The goal is to connect an abstract transformation rule with concrete neural responses and connections in a recurrent circuit.

The authors find that a continuous attractor network generates a continuous family of stationary population responses that represents the stimulus equivariantly. Inspired by the fruit fly's compass circuit, they add speed neurons whose responses encode movement speed. Feedback connections from those neurons to the attractor network represent the generator of translation, the mathematical operation underlying incremental shifts.

This assigns complementary roles to the neural components: the attractor family represents stimulus states, while speed-related activity and feedback implement their translation. The authors demonstrate that the network responses are consistent with experimental data. The model thus supplies a circuit-level account of translation-equivariant representation within the studied one-dimensional setting, linking recurrent dynamics to group transformations.
neurips-2022-translation-equivariant-rep.tldr: A continuous attractor network with speed neurons models how recurrent circuits can represent stimuli equivariantly under one-dimensional translation.

paragraphs: When connected people have similar outcomes, the similarity may reflect influence between them or traits they already share. This paper studies the effect of a treatment applied to one person on their neighbors' outcomes using observational network data. The central obstacle is homophily: shared, unobserved traits can influence both social connections and the outcomes being analyzed.

Because those traits are not directly measured, researchers cannot simply include them as observed adjustment variables. The proposed approach instead uses node embeddings learned from the network itself to perform the required adjustment. Network structure thereby provides information for addressing the hidden common causes that complicate estimates of peer influence.

The authors formalize the causal effect nonparametrically and show how embedding methods can identify and estimate it while accounting for homophily. Their aim is to avoid specifying functional forms for network formation, treatment assignment, or outcomes. The contribution connects representation learning on networks to causal estimation, focusing on separating treatment spillovers from similarities associated with how connections arise.
neurips-2022-using-embeddings-for-causal.tldr: Network embeddings support nonparametric adjustment for homophily when identifying and estimating causal peer-influence effects.

paragraphs: Authorship analysis examines who wrote a text and can support forensic investigation of online activity. However, much previous research used literary material such as novels or fan fiction. VeriDark addresses the concern that such data may not represent the writing encountered in cybercrime investigations, where prior studies have also relied on ad hoc datasets and evaluation setups.

The benchmark contains three large-scale authorship-verification datasets and one authorship-identification dataset. Verification concerns whether texts share an author, while identification concerns assigning authorship. The source material comes from user activity in Dark Web-related Reddit communities or popular illicit Dark Web market forums, bringing the benchmark closer to the stated application context.

The authors evaluate competitive natural-language-processing baselines on the three verification datasets and analyze their predictions to better understand the approaches' limitations. Both datasets and baselines are publicly released. The main contribution is a shared evaluation resource for studying authorship analysis on relevant online writing, accompanied by baseline results and analysis that future methods can build upon.
neurips-2022-veridark-a-large-scale-benc.tldr: VeriDark provides public authorship-analysis datasets and baselines drawn from Dark Web forums and related Reddit communities.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter averages probability distributions while respecting their geometry. This paper presents a generative-model approach to approximating Wasserstein-2 barycenters of continuous distributions. The aim is to retain a meaningful distributional average while avoiding restrictions that have made earlier approaches difficult to scale.

The authors identify two obstacles in previous methods. Entropic or quadratic regularization introduces bias, while input-convex neural networks can lack the expressiveness needed for large-scale tasks. Their proposed algorithm avoids introducing this bias and permits arbitrary neural-network architectures. That flexibility opens the choice of model beyond the input-convex networks used by earlier approaches, while the computational task remains barycenter approximation.

The paper also introduces Ave, celeba!, a dataset constructed from a celebrity-faces dataset for quantitative evaluation of barycenter methods. It enables the use of standard generative-model metrics such as FID. Together, the algorithm and dataset address both how to represent an estimated barycenter and how to evaluate barycenter algorithms using a concrete generative-model benchmark.
neurips-2022-wasserstein-iterative-netwo.tldr: The paper approximates Wasserstein barycenters with unrestricted neural architectures without introducing regularization bias and provides a dataset for evaluation.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection seeks to recognize data outside the distribution a model is expected to handle. Existing methods often use representations from an already trained deep model. This paper explores another property of those models: manipulating data can reprogram their behavior for a new purpose without changing their learned parameters.

The proposed method, called watermarking, learns a single shared pattern and superimposes it on the features of the original data. The pattern is designed to make a classification model more effective at out-of-distribution detection. Learning therefore takes place in the added pattern, while the well-trained model's parameters remain fixed.

The authors report that watermarking substantially boosts detection capability, with extensive experiments supporting its effectiveness. The finding suggests that a classifier's usefulness for detection depends partly on how data are presented to it, not only on its existing representations. The paper's contribution is a general method for exploiting that reprogramming property through a learned, unified feature perturbation.
neurips-2022-watermarking-for-out-of-dis.tldr: A learned shared watermark improves out-of-distribution detection by reprogramming a classifier through its data while keeping model parameters fixed.

paragraphs: Representation learning seeks to recover the hidden variables that generated observed data. This paper studies a weak form of supervision: observations produced when only a sparse subset of latent variables is perturbed. An example is an environment where an action moves an individual sprite. The authors show that such observations can enable identification under unknown continuous latent distributions.

The precision of recovery depends on which variables the perturbations affect together. When perturbations act on mutually exclusive blocks, the latent variables can be identified up to those blocks. When blocks overlap, the guarantee improves to the smallest blocks shared across perturbations, so the pattern of overlap determines which latent distinctions can be recovered.

If some blocks intersect in just one latent variable, those variables can be identified up to permutation and scaling. This is a conditional guarantee tied to perturbation structure, rather than unrestricted exact recovery. The authors propose an estimation procedure based on the theory and illustrate it with low-dimensional synthetic and image-based experiments.
neurips-2022-weakly-supervised-represent.tldr: Sparse latent perturbations enable identification under unknown continuous distributions, with recovery precision determined by how perturbation blocks overlap.

paragraphs: Conventional saliency maps highlight input features that strongly affect a model's prediction. This paper instead investigates which network parameters are associated with incorrect decisions. Its parameter-space saliency maps aim to locate internal components involved in errors, providing a different perspective on why a model misclassifies particular samples.

The authors validate the identified parameters through interventions. Disabling salient parameters improves predictions on the associated samples more than disabling an equal number of randomly chosen or least-salient parameters. They also find that fine-tuning a small set of highly salient parameters on one sample can correct errors on other samples nearby in saliency space.

Those neighboring samples were misclassified for similar reasons, linking shared parameter involvement to related failures. The authors further demonstrate that samples associated with similar malfunctioning parameters are semantically similar. An additional input-space saliency method reveals which image features cause particular network components to malfunction. Together, these analyses connect observable image content, internal parameters, and patterns of prediction error.
neurips-2022-where-do-models-go-wrong-pa.tldr: Parameter-space saliency identifies network components involved in errors and links them to semantically related failures across samples.
